summary: Overall the course is accurate and well pitched for Year 1. All numeric keys (pack-years, units, MAP, cuff width, deoxy-Hb, JVP, compression time and fraction, blood loss, hand-hygiene compliance) were recomputed and are correct, every MCQ has exactly one correct option matching the key, and clinical content (WHO five moments, UK Resuscitation Council BLS and choking sequence, inguinal/femoral landmarks, tracheal deviation, cyanosis threshold) checks out. One major problem: the abdominal auscultation lesson gives a self-contradictory rationale for the order of examination. The remaining issues are minor internal inconsistencies and one omission in first-aid bleeding control. This is an AI review only; the course still needs a subject-matter expert before clinical reliance.

issues.problem: Lesson says the abdominal order "differs from the rest of the body because palpation and percussion can alter bowel activity, so listening is traditionally done after the hands-on phases". The stated rationale argues for the opposite: that concern is the reason many schemes (inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation) listen before palpation. The statement is internally illogical and could teach students a wrong reason.
issues.suggestedFix: State accurately that some schemes auscultate before palpation and percussion precisely because touch may alter bowel sounds, while other (e.g. UK OSCE) schemes place auscultation after palpation and percussion for consistency with other systems. Tell students to follow their school's scheme. Align with the inspect-palpate-percuss ordering in the previous unit and check wording against a standard clinical skills text.

issues.problem: Guarding is defined as "voluntary or involuntary tightening of the abdominal wall muscles", and the table lists guarding as "local peritoneal irritation", but the key-point callout, q003 and q008 treat voluntary tensing as distinct from true (reflex) guarding.
issues.suggestedFix: Define guarding as involuntary (reflex) muscle contraction due to peritoneal irritation and name voluntary tensing separately as a confounder.

issues.problem: Explanation says "a heart rate above 100 ... outside typical ranges" and treats pulse 118 as abnormal, but the lesson's table gives pulse as "concerning if below 50 or above 120". The key remains right (RR 26, temp 38.6), but the pulse threshold conflicts with the lesson.
issues.suggestedFix: Either align the lesson table (tachycardia above 100, concerning thresholds per local early-warning score) or reword the explanation to rest on the respiratory rate and temperature.

issues.problem: Lesson says to count the radial pulse "for at least 15 to 30 seconds", whereas the vital signs unit teaches 30 seconds doubled or 60 seconds if irregular.
issues.suggestedFix: Use the same instruction as the vital signs unit (30 seconds and double, or 60 seconds if irregular).

issues.problem: Bleeding control teaches direct pressure only. Current UK Resuscitation Council first aid guidance also includes a tourniquet (and haemostatic dressing) for life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by direct pressure. The unit uses arterial injury and 21% blood loss examples (q007) without mentioning this escalation. Unverified against the exact current edition; recommend a source check.
issues.suggestedFix: Add a short note that for catastrophic limb haemorrhage not controlled by firm direct pressure, a tourniquet applied by a trained or instructed rescuer is the next step, and that emergency services must be called.

issues.problem: Stem asks for "the minimum required" items, but the lesson lists patient identifiers as the first required element and the key option (a) omits them. The key is still the best option among the distractors.
issues.suggestedFix: Add patient identifiers to option (a), or reword the stem to "Which set best describes the key elements of an entry's authorship and timing".
